submission.natural_language_explanation: Broad head: it rests on the text's first token (strength near 0) and turns active when it attends with weight near 1 to one recent item instead, most strongly (about 0.45-0.9 x max) on the separator right after a number in a citation or numeric list (the ',' or '-' in '[3,5]' or '[3-5]', the '][' or ' [' between citations, the ',' after ' 3' in 'were 3, 5, 7', the newline before the next numbered line) and on the separator (',' or ' and') after the SECOND or later common-noun item of a list ('eggs, milk,' -> the second comma); the separator after a first word item stays weak. Predict INACTIVE (below 0.25 x max) for bare two-item pairs of 3-4 tokens with no other words ('bread and butter', 'gold, silver', 'Tom and Mary') and for short sentences whose only list-like element is one single-number citation such as 'See [7] for details.' or 'Our study [4] confirms this.'; longer ordinary prose is mixed (some content words cross weakly) and is not claimed either way.

rival_explanations: Broader: the head fires wherever its attention leaves the first token for any recent content word, separator or not, so unpunctuated runs ('He likes cats dogs birds now') and lists of proper names ('Tom, Ann, Bob, Sue') should be as active as comma lists of common nouns.

Narrower: the head is a numeric-item tracker that fires only on separators after numbers (citations, numeric lists, numbered lines), so comma lists of plain words such as 'eggs, milk, flour' should stay inactive.
